FEP × Physics via Non‑Equilibrium Steady States (NESS)

FEP connects to physics by assuming organisms occupy a NESS

Why NESS matters for the Free‑Energy Principle

Living systems are open and far from thermodynamic equilibrium. Yet their states remain confined to a narrow set (they persist). In physics, this is modelled as a non‑equilibrium steady state (NESS): probability densities over system states stop changing in time (stationary), even while energy and matter flow through the system and entropy is produced. The FEP links to this by identifying the negative log of the stationary density with surprisal (self‑information). If internal states flow down the gradients of this quantity (subject to constraints set by the agent’s interface with the world), they will, on average, avoid surprise and remain in the small set of “life‑supporting” states.

From stochastic dynamics to a steady‑state density

  • Langevin dynamics: continuous‑time stochastic dynamics \dot{s}=f(s)+\omega(t) with diffusion D imply a Fokker–Planck equation for the density \rho(s,t).
  • Stationarity: at NESS, \partial_t\rho=0 and \nabla\cdot J=0, where J=f\rho-D\nabla\rho is probability current. Detailed balance is generally broken (nonzero curl component/circulation), so there is sustained entropy production.
  • Non‑equilibrium potential: define \mathcal U(s) = -\ln \rho_{\!*}(s). This is a Lyapunov‑like function whose gradients favour return to high‑probability (low‑surprisal) regions.

Markov blankets: separating inside from outside

To make “inference” a property of internal states, FEP introduces a Markov blanket: a set of sensory and active variables that shield internal variables from external ones. Under mild assumptions (ergodicity, time‑scale separation), internal states come to encode conditional densities over external states, i.e. they behave like a Bayesian posterior under a generative model. This provides the bridge from physics (NESS) to computation (variational inference).

Variational free energy as a tractable proxy

Exact surprisal -\ln p(o) is intractable, so organisms minimise an upper bound—variational free energy—by updating approximate posteriors q and model parameters. This yields predictive‑coding style updates (precision‑weighted errors), while action is chosen by minimising expected free energy, which decomposes into risk/ambiguity (or extrinsic/epistemic) terms.

Thermodynamic intuition

  • Broken detailed balance: NESSs generate positive entropy production (housekeeping heat) to maintain order.
  • Landscape & flux: flows can be decomposed into gradient descent on the non‑equilibrium potential plus a solenoidal (circulatory) component.
  • Homeostasis ↔ allostasis: organisms regulate around a set‑distribution, not a single set‑point; priors/preferences encode that distribution.

Assumptions, scope, caveats

  • Steady‑state idealisation: real organisms face changing niches; NESS is often a metastable approximation over relevant timescales.
  • Blanket identification: mapping real mechanisms to a formal Markov blanket can be nontrivial; ongoing debates refine when and how blankets apply.
  • Falsifiability resides in models: the principle constrains model classes; concrete active‑inference models are tested against data.
